note: The same facts as README.md's Install section, in a shape a screen can render. Gates keep the two identical; edit both or neither.

reminders.what: Check what you already know before answering
Save what settled, and say in one line what was saved
reminders.when: with your next message, once enough has accumulated

reminders.what: Get put back on track after a long conversation forgets itself

spokenSentences.text: [Dazzer] Before answering anything your Brain may already know, recall it - answer from what is recorded, not from assumption. If you cannot reach the Brain, say so plainly - never present files, transcripts or guesses as what it holds. As real decisions accumulate in this session, checkpoint your progress so a context reset cannot lose your place.

[Dazzer] This session restarted from a context reset, so nothing reconnected and you were never re-oriented. Call resume to restore your saved working session before continuing, and before asking the user to repeat anything.

verify.what: One line written every time the plugin runs, recording when, what it decided and why — never any of your conversation.
verify.emptyMeans: The plugin has never run — worth knowing, because that failure is otherwise completely silent.

tools.name: Claude Code
tools.describedAs: Anthropic’s coding tool, separate from the Claude desktop app

installReminders.note: Typed into Claude itself, not into your shell.

surfaces.label: The desktop app
surfaces.note: Install it from a terminal with the same two lines. The app and the terminal share one set of settings, so it appears in the app on your next conversation. The install command does not exist inside the app, so this genuinely needs a terminal once — even if you never otherwise open one.

installReminders.note: Codex asks you to approve a plugin's reminders before it will run them. If nothing appears in the run history, that approval is the first thing to check.

tools.name: GitHub Copilot

installReminders.note: This tool gives a reminder no way to speak to the model - it can watch and it can block, and nothing it says is passed on. Proven by running one: both moments fired and every shape of reply was discarded. So the check-first reminder is delivered as a standing instruction instead, which this tool reads before every conversation, and the third step above is what puts it there. The other two reminders need a moment AND a voice, so they stay undelivered here.

limits: Two of the three reminders do not arrive. Saving what settled at the end of a reply, and being put back on track after a long conversation forgets itself, both need to speak at a particular moment, and this tool lets a reminder do only one of those. Checking your Brain before answering is the one that survives, and it is the one that matters most.
The standing instruction is a copy, not a link - this tool ignores a link. So re-run the third install step after updating the plugin, or the copy keeps whatever wording it first got.

The standing instruction has to TELL the model what to do, not remind it. The first version opened by explaining to a human why reminders cannot work here, and the model read that explanation as part of its instruction: asked six times whether it would check the Brain unprompted, it did so none of those times. Rewritten as a plain instruction naming what to call and when, it did so all six. Anything added to that file is read by the model, so commentary belongs in the README, never there.

tools.name: Antigravity

installReminders.note: This tool cannot read the main plugin's reminders file, because it and Devin both look for a file of that name and want different shapes inside it - and this tool discards a whole file over one entry it does not recognise, exactly as Claude Code does. Proven by putting both shapes in one file and watching every reminder vanish. So its reminders ship as a second small plugin of their own, which the third step installs. A broken neighbour sitting beside it does not take it down; that was proven too. The second plugin carries no copy of the end-of-reply script - it runs the one the first plugin already ships, which is why both are installed.

limits: Being put back on track after a long conversation forgets itself was never possible here - that moment does not exist in this tool.
gotchas: This tool never says whether a reply is the one our own save prompt asked for, which every other tool does say. Leaning on the amount of new work instead was tried and measured wrong - the prompt fired five times in one reply and the answer repeated five times - so the prompt now leaves itself a note that the very next reply reads once and clears. The cost is that a genuine second reply straight after a save is skipped, which is the safe direction.

tools.name: Cursor
tools.describedAs: a code editor with an AI built into it

installReminders.note: Two steps, and the second one happens inside Cursor rather than in a terminal.

limits: Cursor has no way for a plugin to speak privately to the AI at the end of a reply. It only accepts a message and submits it as though you had typed it, so on Cursor the save prompt is visible in your conversation. The save prompt still does its job; it just is not silent.
gotchas: If you have installed it before, remove and re-add rather than update. Cursor's update command reports success without actually re-fetching, so you keep whatever version you first got. Run `cursor-agent plugin marketplace remove dazzer` then add it again.
If you already have some other Dazzer setup wired into Cursor, take it out first, or both fire on every reply and you get the save prompt twice.

tools.name: Devin
limits: Two of the three reminders work. The save prompt does not, and cannot: Devin tells a reminder only which session and which prompt it is, with no way to tell how much conversation has built up since last time. The prompt has nothing to measure, so it stays quiet rather than firing blindly.

tools.name: Claude (chat app and web)
tools.describedAs: the Claude you already chat with, in the app or a browser tab
limits: Claude's chat apps and the web app have no moment at the end of a reply for anything to run. There the bundled skill carries the same intent as plain text, and reaching your Brain works exactly the same.

installConnection.askFirst: Nothing — run it whether or not you already have Dazzer.
installConnection.skipWhen: Never. Running it again is how you get the current version.
installConnection.warning: You will be asked to sign in again afterwards. That is the point: installing does not sign you in, and the sign-in is what was missing.
installConnection.note: Everything above adds the reminders. They do not reach your Brain by themselves, so a tool with the reminders and no connection has an AI being told to check something it cannot open. One line per tool below, in that tool's own wording.

claude-code.proven: run on a clean Claude Code; it registers the connection and asks to sign in

codex.proven: run on a clean Codex; `codex mcp list` then shows dazzer with a sign-in waiting

claude-code.note: Only a machine that has never had Dazzer gets a sign-in during the install. On every other machine nothing happens at all — watched, 2026-08-10. Close the tool and start it again, then sign in when it asks. If it does not ask, open the sign-in list yourself.
claude-code.proven: watched: already installed, so the install was silent and no sign-in ever appeared

codex.note: Nothing appears when the connection installs. Without this the first thing that reaches your Brain fails, quietly.

copilot.note: Close the tool and start it again, then sign in when it asks. Watched, 2026-08-10: the sign-in appeared on the next start, not during the install.
copilot.proven: watched: sign-in appeared the next time the tool was started

devin.note: Close the tool and start it again, then sign in when it asks. Watched, 2026-08-10: it signed in without asking and worked. If yours does ask, this is when.
devin.proven: watched: signed in silently on first use and reached the Brain

antigravity.note: Close the tool and start it again, then sign in when it asks. Watched, 2026-08-10: it never reached the Brain at all. If asking it what your Brain knows comes back with anything other than real records, it is not signed in.

cursor.note: Close the tool and start it again, then sign in when it asks. Not established on this tool.

provenance.what: All six were installed into a real copy of the tool and watched working, which proved too little: on three of them nothing reached the AI at all - Codex and Cursor discarded the words, and Claude Code never loaded the plugin. Proving the words arrive from a hand-written file proved too little in turn, because it says nothing about whether the shipped file loads, and a tool reporting its own reminders as registered proved nothing either - it says so even when it is delivering nothing. What counts is installing the real thing and asking the AI for a word only the reminder carried. Claude Code and Cursor each answer it. Codex runs every reminder from an installed copy, which is the weaker evidence of the two. Devin takes the plain wording it already gets. Antigravity and Copilot are given no reminders at all rather than ones that would be silently dead.

keepCurrent.why: Nothing updates on its own. Sources like ours have automatic updating switched off by default, so a person stays on whatever version they first installed until they do something about it.

claude-code.note: All three, in that order, then restart. The first refreshes the list of what exists and does NOTHING to the plugin being used - it prints a success message either way, which is how a person ran it, restarted, and got the old behaviour back. Only the update lines move the version actually in use. Drop the third where the connection was never installed separately. To stop doing it by hand, open the plugin panel with /plugin, go to Marketplaces, choose dazzer, turn on auto-update.
claude-code.proven: watched: 0.8.3 to 0.9.0 on a real machine, after the marketplace command had reported success and changed nothing

antigravity.note: Then run the same three install lines again against the refreshed copy.

cursor.note: Then add it again and install. Cursors update command reports success without re-fetching, so removing and re-adding is the only thing that genuinely gets a newer version.
cursor.proven: watched: a machine sat on an old version while reporting itself up to date
